title: Damayanti
html:
The Sister of Raghava Pandita

In Panihati, by the Ganga, lived Raghava Pandita, one of Sri Chaitanya's first followers, and with him his sister Damayanti. Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls her “a dear maidservant of the Lord” (prabhura priya dasi); the biographies call her Damayanti and Damayanti Devi, and Narahari Chakravarti “loving (snehavati) Damayanti Devi.”1 A line of the “Shripata-paryatana,” verses on the holy places (shripatas) of Gauda ascribed to Abhirama Thakura, remembers brother and sister:

“In the village of Panihati is the abode of Raghava and Damayanti; of it the tale is told that goes by the name ‘Raghava's jhalis.’”

So their home entered the memory of Gauda: through the hampers (jhalis) that left it every year for Nilachala, for the Lord.

Of the rest of her life the sources tell almost nothing. Neither the year and day of her appearance are known, nor when and where she left this world; nor are her days found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math — as her brother's days are not found there either. Yet of her service to the Lord Krishnadasa Kaviraja tells in greater detail than of almost anyone's: a whole part of a chapter of the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” he gave to a single list of what she prepared for Mahaprabhu.

Gunamala

Who she is in Krishna's eternal pastimes, Kavi Karnapura tells us. First, of her brother:

“Sri Kashishvara Gosvami is the former Shashirekha in Vraja. Dhanishtha, who in Vraja gave Krishna countless delicacies, is now Raghava Pandita, dear to Gauranga.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 166)

And next, of her:

“She who in Vraja was Gunamala is Damayanti, his sister.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 167)

So the biographies identify her, and so does Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in his “Anubhashya” on CC Adi 10.25. Gunamala is a gopi of Vraja; she who served Krishna in Vraja came into Gaura's pastimes together with the Lord and together with her brother, whose service in Vraja too was in delicacies for Krishna. What her flavour of service (rasa) is in Vraja, Karnapura does not say, and we shall not name it: her care for the Lord, of which we shall speak below, is touching and full of tenderness, but the sources give no ground for counting it either as parental or as friendly love. It is enough that Kavi Karnapura named her among the eternal associates.

“A Dear Maidservant of the Lord”

Krishnadasa Kaviraja, listing the branches of Sri Chaitanya's tree, names Raghava, his disciple Makaradhvaja and his sister:

“Raghava Pandita was one of the Lord's first followers, and his chief branch is Makaradhvaja Kara. His sister Damayanti, a dear maidservant of the Lord, prepared provisions for Him all year round. Filling bags with all those provisions, Raghava would carry them secretly to the Lord. All year round the Lord accepted them, and they became famous as ‘Raghava's bags.’” (CC, Adi 10.24–27)

And he adds:

“I shall describe those provisions in detail later. Hearing of them, the devotees shed streams of tears.” (CC, Adi 10.28)

All twelve months of the year (vara-masi) Damayanti cooked for the Lord, and her offerings were so many that they lasted Him a whole year. She did not simply cook: she considered which dish would do the Lord good at which season, and in each season she prepared what was fitting. Long-keeping pickles (niskri — made without water or boiled rice), other foods and gathered provisions for His daily meals she lovingly packed into boxes and bags and sent to Nilachala with Raghava and other devotees. Every year Raghava brought the Lord countless foods dear to Him, prepared by his sister, and Krishnadasa Kaviraja described them in the tenth chapter of the “Antya-lila.”

Damayanti and Raghava knew Mahaprabhu to be the Supreme Lord Himself. Yet so strong was the love they bore Him that she cared for His health as one cares for someone near and dear. She cooked at her brother's bidding (ajna), and Kaviraja says of them both:

“Raghava gave the orders, and Damayanti carried them out. Both had deep affection and supreme devotion for the Lord.” (CC, Antya 10.34)

All this was not household work but the service (seva) of an eternal associate. What she prepared was an offering (naivedya) to the Lord; what remained from Him Kaviraja calls prasada.

Raghava's Jhalis

Every year in the month of Ashadha, for the Ratha-yatra, the devotees of Gauda travelled to Puri for the Lord's darshan, and each brought something for His service. With them went Raghava Pandita with his hampers. Damayanti prepared what was in them, and Raghava carried them and secretly brought them to the Lord:

“Raghava Pandita set out with his jhalis (hampers), packed with all the things that Damayanti had prepared and given him. There were many wonderful foods, offerings worthy of the Lord, enough for Him to partake of for a whole year.” (CC, Antya 10.13–14)

Whether she herself went to Puri, the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” does not say.2

When everything was ready, Damayanti packed the jhalis herself, and here her care reached down to the smallest things:

“She brought clay from the Ganga, strained it through cloth, mixed in fragrant substances and made it into panch-kudi (thin wafers). She filled thin clay pots with sandalwood paste and other things, and packed everything else in little cloth bags. She made jhalis twice the size of ordinary ones and neatly filled them all. She tied up the jhalis and carefully sealed them. Three porters carried them, taking turns.” (CC, Antya 10.35–38)

The seal was set on the jhalis so that no stranger would open them on the way.

“I have briefly described these jhalis, which became famous as ‘Raghava's jhalis.’” (CC, Antya 10.39)

By that name — “Raghava's jhalis” — her service has remained in the memory of the Vaishnavas. On the road they were guarded by Raghava's disciple Makaradhvaja Kara of Panihati:

“Makaradhvaja Kara was the munsib (steward) of the jhalis; he guarded them vigilantly, as if they were his very life.” (CC, Antya 10.40)

As their steward he brought them to Puri every year with great diligence.3

What Was in the Jhalis

Krishnadasa Kaviraja gives almost in full the list of what Damayanti prepared for the Lord. It opens with relishes and tart pickles:

“There were mango kashandi and the relishes called ginger and chili kashandi, lime and ginger with mango buds, and other preparations; amsi, ama-khanda, tailamra (mango pickle in mustard oil) and ama-satta; and dried shukta (bitter greens), carefully ground into powder.” (CC, Antya 10.15–16)

Then come ladus of coriander and anise cooked in sugar syrup; ginger with sugar and remedies for indigestion and excess bile, each in its own little bag; kul berries in various forms (koli-shunthi, koli-churna, koli-khanda) and a hundred kinds of pickles; coconut sweets and white gangajali balls, like the waters of the Ganga; long-keeping khirsa, sweets of milk and cream, amrita-karpura; a whole bag of new cloth full of flat rice (chida) from sun-dried shali paddy; hurum fried in ghee and cooked in syrup with camphor; ladus of ground fried shali rice with camphor, black pepper, cloves and cardamom; ukhra of popped rice (khai); ladus of fried peas (CC, Antya 10.22–32). And Kaviraja ends humbly:

“There were a thousand kinds of such foods, whose names I could not tell in this lifetime.” (CC, Antya 10.33)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati remarks in the “Anubhashya” that this description shows how skilled Krishnadasa Kaviraja himself was in preparing offerings for Krishna. One of the biographies repeats this thought.4 And in the words “whose names I could not tell” one hears Kaviraja's own humility.

Shukta

Among all these sweets and pickles was one humble thing — shukta, dried bitter greens ground to powder. Of it Kaviraja speaks especially:

“Do not look down on it because it is only shukta: the joy found in shukta is not found even in panchamrita. Mahaprabhu receives the feeling (bhava-grahi): it is the affection alone that He accepts. So the shukta leaves and kashandi gave Him great joy. Damayanti, in her affection, regarded the Lord as a human being (manushya-buddhi): ‘From heavy food, ama (indigestion) may sometimes form in His stomach. If He eats shukta, that ama will be cured.’ Thinking of her affection, the Lord was delighted.” (CC, Antya 10.17–20)

Damayanti feared that rich, heavy food might harm the Lord and cause Him indigestion (ama).5 Against this she prepared her shukta. Kaviraja says that she saw the Lord “as a human being” (manushya-buddhi). This is not worldly ignorance, nor doubt of His divinity: she knew who He is. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that this is how the people of Gauda and Vraja love the Lord — with a natural (svarasiki) love. Their hearts, made of pure goodness, do not remember His majesty (aishvarya), and they know Gaura-Krishna in His human form as one conquered by their pure love. That is why Bhaktisiddhanta heads these verses: the evidence of Damayanti's pure, natural and extraordinarily deep love for Gaura. Love surpasses the knowledge of majesty: even knowing that before her was the Supreme Lord Himself, she cared for Him as for one dear to her, who needed her care.

And the Lord is bhava-grahi, He who receives the feeling. He accepts not the thing but the love with which it is offered, and so the plain bitter shukta pleased Him more than panchamrita. Nor was it only the taste that pleased Him: thinking of Damayanti's love, He rejoiced. The bhava spoken of here, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains in the “Anubhashya,” is not a worldly movement of the mind seeking its own pleasure, as with the prakrita-sahajiyas, but a causeless, transcendental movement of the heart, born of pure goodness (shuddha-sattva) and turned only to Krishna's joy.

How the Lord Accepted Her Service

Having brought the jhalis to Puri, Raghava handed them to the Lord's servant Govinda:

“Raghava handed the jhalis over to Govinda, and they were kept in a corner of the dining room. Govinda emptied the previous year's jhalis and took them to another room, keeping them there to be filled with provisions.” (CC, Antya 10.55–56)

The Lord did not hurry to open them. When He had tasted all the foods brought by the other devotees and asked whether anything more was left, Govinda replied: “Only Raghava's jhalis are left.” The Lord said that He would not touch them that day and would look at them later (CC, Antya 10.127–128). On another day He opened them Himself:

“Another day, when the Lord ate in seclusion, He opened Raghava's jhalis and looked at everything. He tasted a little of every item and, finding them delicious and fragrant, praised them highly. The rest He kept in store for a whole year, and at mealtimes Svarupa would take out a little and serve it. Sometimes, at night too, Svarupa would have Him partake of a little; for the Lord surely enjoys what a devotee gives with faith (shraddha).” (CC, Antya 10.129–132)

So Govinda kept Damayanti's provisions, and Svarupa Damodara served them at the Lord's meals.6 “The Harmonist,” published under the editorship of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, writes that Govinda with great care gave the Lord to taste the foods constantly sent by Raghava Pandita and Damayanti. Thus Mahaprabhu, who receives the feeling, accepted all year round the loving service of brother and sister.

Here lies the secret of her service. The wish to please Krishna's senses — that is prema:

“The desire to please one's own senses is called lust (kama); the wish to please Krishna's senses bears the name of prema.” (CC, Adi 4.165)

And so a devotee, offering the Lord his gift, seeks not his own joy but His alone.7 Damayanti spent months thinking of what would do the Lord good and what would please Him — and of herself the sources have kept not a word.

Her Memory

Narahari Chakravarti, in the song that concludes the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” prays to serve, birth after birth, the feet of the Lord's associates, and names among them Madhava Mishra and Ratnavati, Malini, Madhavi and “loving Damayanti Devi.” And in the opening of his “Namamrita-samudra” he calls to the Lord's women associates:

“O Madhavi, Malini, Damayanti, O Sri Sita! Who but you is Gauranga's protector?”

Significance

Damayanti did not preach or write books, and the stories about her are few. But Krishnadasa Kaviraja called her “a dear maidservant of the Lord” and gave a whole part of a chapter to her offerings, and the devotees, he says, weep to hear of them. Her life was a service of love: all year long she thought of the Lord, of what was good for Him and what would gladden Him, and she put that thought into every little bag. Bitter shukta offered with such love proved dearer to the Lord than panchamrita, for He accepts the feeling, not the thing. Her care for Him, as for one near and dear, is not ignorance but the natural love of the people of Gauda and Vraja, before which the knowledge of His majesty grows dim. With this love Damayanti won the Lord: thinking of it, He rejoiced.

Notes

  1. In our edition of the Russian translation of the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” the name is spelled differently in Adi 10 (“Damayyanti”) and in Antya 10 (“Damayanti”). In this article the name is given uniformly as Damayanti, and an obvious slip in the Russian of Adi 10.25 is corrected. Raghava's hampers are called “Raghava's bags” in Adi 10.27 and “Raghava's jhalis” in Antya 10.39.
  2. One of the biographies says that Damayanti herself carried the jhalis to Puri and offered them to the Lord. But according to the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” it was Raghava who carried the bags and secretly brought them to the Lord (Adi 10.26; Antya 10.13), and he who handed them to Govinda (Antya 10.55); and the same biography says elsewhere that she sent them through Raghava and others. We follow the primary source: she prepared, Raghava carried; of any journeys of her own to Puri the sources are silent.
  3. One of the biographies says that Makaradhvaja carried to Puri the bags prepared by his spiritual master, that is, by Raghava. This is inexact: they were prepared by Damayanti (CC, Adi 10.25–26; Antya 10.13–14, 10.34), while Raghava fitted them out and carried them.
  4. That biography's words on Kaviraja's skill, as on “Damayanti's extraordinarily deep love for Gaura” (see below), repeat the “Anubhashya” on Antya 10.13–39 and 10.19, though without naming it.
  5. One of the biographies renders ama as “dysentery” and says that shukta “reduces phlegm.” According to the “Anubhashya,” ama is an acid-bilious disorder (amla-pitta) arising from indigestion when the digestive fire is weakened.
  6. According to one of the biographies, Govinda not only kept her provisions but also gave the Lord a little of them every day at His meals. According to the “Chaitanya-charitamrita,” Govinda received and kept the bags (Antya 10.55–56), while it was Svarupa Damodara who served them to the Lord all year round (Antya 10.131). There is no real contradiction: one kept, the other served.
  7. One of the biographies develops this thought, citing Adi 4.165 without a reference and from memory (vanchha, “wish,” instead of ichchha in the text of the “Chaitanya-charitamrita”).
